targets.title: The dark side of self-and social perception: Black uniforms and aggression in professional sports
targets.evidence_quote: The first goal of the current investigation was to attempt to conceptually replicate Frank and Gilovich’s (1988) NFL archival work but also to address major flaws in the original study.
targets.outcome_quote: Regardless of why the effect was transpiring, the foundation of the association in their research was built upon their archival study of both the NFL and the NHL, which we failed to replicate in both leagues.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The overall author verdict explicitly reports failure in both leagues, despite some individual positive modern NHL contrasts.

targets.authors: Webster, G. D., Urland, G. R., & Correll, J.
targets.title: Can uniform color color aggression? Quasi-experimental evidence from professional ice hockey
targets.evidence_quote: We now extend our investigation to the modern NHL while attempting to address deficiencies in past research which supported the black uniforms-heightened aggression connection.
targets.outcome_quote: Also, we failed to find support for reduced aggression when wearing white uniforms (Webster et al., 2012) as we conducted comparisons within teams across eight seasons while ensuring the overall aggression in the league remained consistent (thus avoiding a history threat).
targets.outcome_reasoning: Study III directly addresses the modern NHL black-uniform and white-uniform findings, discusses methodological deficiencies in Webster, and reports failure for the white effect as well as the nested black-uniform analysis.

reasoning: New archival samples in Studies I and III are replications; Study II reconstructs the earlier period and discusses its threats. Two original papers are retested. Caldwell and Burger is contextual earlier evidence, not an independently selected target. Study II does not establish a successful overall replication and the authors explicitly give a failure verdict.
